Historical identity / living descendants

Jumano

Spanish and later sources used “Jumano” for peoples across Texas, New Mexico, and adjacent northern Mexico. Scholars disagree whether it named one distinct people, several groups, or a broader label; contemporary Jumano community accounts describe living descendants. This profile keeps historical classifications and present-day community identity separate.

Names & relationshipsThe historical label Jumano appears in sources for different peoples and settings. This entry also links to contemporary Jumano community accounts and a separate Indigenous-led La Junta organization that names Jumano among several descendant communities. These relationships are presented with their own source scope; they do not establish that every historical use names one polity, or that one modern organization represents everyone connected to the name.
A cited introduction, with more to explore.This overview draws together the linked sources below. It is an introduction, and does not replace community-authored histories or a full scholarly study.
Not assessed

Seven distinct substantive resources have actual-content inspection records: scholarly and educational syntheses, a complete early journal article, selected excerpts from a limited-access monograph, a local report quoting a Jumano historian, and an Indigenous-led La Junta organization’s own description. Five supporting records are kept outside the substantive count. This is a useful initial reading path, but historical identifications, contemporary community coverage, and primary-record access remain too limited to judge adequacy.

Assessment recorded October 23, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

01

A historical name with contested scope

Records from the sixteenth through eighteenth centuries use Jumano across several regions and contexts. The Handbook of Texas summarizes at least three groupings sometimes associated with the name: Tompiro-speaking Pueblo communities in New Mexico, mobile traders around the Rio Grande and Conchos, and Wichita-speaking peoples whom Spanish writers also called Jumano. Nancy Hickerson argues that the label often referred to a distinct trading people, while J. Charles Kelley and other scholars distinguish particular Jumano groups from the settled Patarabueye communities at La Junta. These are scholarly models built from uneven colonial records, not settled identifications for every named group.

Read the sources [3] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online [4] Texas Beyond History [6] University of Michigan Press / Museum of Anthropological Archaeology; digital edition at JSTOR [9] Texas Beyond History

02

Trade, diplomacy, and a changing borderlands

Spanish accounts and later scholarship describe Jumano travel and trade linking the South Plains, lower Pecos, Rio Grande, New Mexico, and communities farther east. The record includes agricultural and buffalo products, exchanges with Pueblo and Caddo communities, and diplomacy associated with Juan Sabeata. These accounts were produced within colonial expeditions and mission systems. Bolton’s 1911 study reconstructs a longer southern Texas presence than some earlier writers did, but its route identifications and conclusions remain a dated scholarly interpretation rather than direct testimony from the people described.

Read the sources [3] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online [4] Texas Beyond History [5] Quarterly of the Texas State Historical Association 15, pp. 66–84; scan hosted by Wikimedia Commons from an Internet Archive digitization [6] University of Michigan Press / Museum of Anthropological Archaeology; digital edition at JSTOR

03

La Junta was a crossroads, not a single people

La Junta de los Ríos, at the Río Conchos–Río Grande confluence, was home to settled farming communities and a meeting place for mobile peoples. Scholarship uses Patarabueye for some of the village communities and describes Jumano visitors and trading partners; terminology and relationships remain debated. A modern archaeological history emphasizes that the Spanish record has long gaps and that group names are difficult to match confidently to archaeological remains. The region’s history should not be collapsed into one ethnic label.

Read the sources [6] University of Michigan Press / Museum of Anthropological Archaeology; digital edition at JSTOR [9] Texas Beyond History [3] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online

04

What the colonial record can—and cannot—show

Spanish documents are the main written evidence used by the works in this collection. They describe encounters, trade, missions, conflict, and shifting alliances, but they were written by outsiders for colonial purposes and often apply inconsistent names. Bolton quotes documents held in Mexican archives, yet those manuscripts were not inspected for this update. Kelley’s book was available only through selected JSTOR excerpts. A National Archives guide points readers to records; its short entry is not a history or a current determination of a living community’s legal status.

Read the sources [4] Texas Beyond History [5] Quarterly of the Texas State Historical Association 15, pp. 66–84; scan hosted by Wikimedia Commons from an Internet Archive digitization [6] University of Michigan Press / Museum of Anthropological Archaeology; digital edition at JSTOR [2] National Archives

05

Living communities and contemporary accounts

A 2021 local newspaper report records Jumano Nation of Texas historian Felix Bonilla Salmeron describing the nation’s effort to connect with descendants and rejecting the claim that Jumano people disappeared. This is a dated, attributed community perspective reported by a journalist, not a census or an independently verified genealogy. Separately, the Indigenous-led People of La Junta for Preservation describes its descendant communities as including Jumano, Julime, Chisos, Concho, Lipan Apache, and others, and explains its stewardship work at La Junta. That organization’s broader community scope is not interchangeable with the Jumano Nation of Texas.

Read the sources [7] Big Bend Sentinel [8] People of La Junta for Preservation [12] Humanities Texas

06

Reading claims about disappearance and recognition

Some scholarly summaries say that the historical record stops naming Jumano as a distinct people by the late eighteenth century; this documents a limit in surviving records and a scholarly interpretation, not the disappearance of descendants. Contemporary accounts use different evidence and describe continuing identity. Texas House Resolution 1565 honored the Jumano Indian Nation of Texas in 2019; the resolution is a state legislative expression of honor, not a federal recognition decision. Its historical narrative and population claim are not repeated here as independently verified facts. Further community-authored history and archival research are needed.

Read the sources [3] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online [4] Texas Beyond History [7] Big Bend Sentinel [1] Texas Legislature

HR 1565 — Jumano Indians of Texas ↗

The enrolled Texas House resolution documents a state legislative expression honoring the Jumano Indian Nation of Texas. Its historical narrative and population claim are not independent verification and it is not a federal recognition decision.

Inspection scope: The enrolled resolution text was read. It is counted as a supporting primary civic record, not as a substantive historical study.

Academic / referenceTexas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas OnlineSource 3

Jumano Indians ↗

A substantial scholarly state-history synthesis with a bibliography. It describes several different historical groupings associated with Jumano and reviews documentary geography, trade, and migration. Its conclusion that Jumano ceased to exist as an identifiable distinct people is an interpretation of the surviving colonial record; it does not establish that descendants disappeared.

Inspection scope: The full visible article and bibliography were read, including sections on La Junta, Tompiro communities, trade, and the article’s conclusion. The works in its bibliography and original Spanish records were not independently inspected.

Content checked October 23, 2026

Academic / educationalTexas Beyond HistorySource 4

Who Were the Jumano? / Jumano-Spanish Relations ↗

An educational exhibit that synthesizes Spanish accounts of trade, diplomacy, missions, and conflict. Its author explicitly adopts the interpretation that Jumano was a distinct nation. The later statement that Jumano culture was gone and the treatment of biological ‘blood’ are dated outsider interpretations that conflict with contemporary community accounts and should not be presented as established fact.

Inspection scope: Both substantive Jumano modules and the credits page were read. The exhibit’s embedded translations and secondary figures were inspected as presented; cited books, dissertation, article, archives, and maps were not independently reviewed.

The Jumano Indians in Texas, 1650–1771 ↗

A full, early scholarly article arguing that Jumano groups remained in southern Texas into the eighteenth century and that the name was also applied to Taovayas/Wichita people. Read as a dated intervention in an identity debate, not current consensus. The article contains OCR errors and relies on colonial documents; cited manuscript originals were not inspected.

Inspection scope: The complete 26-page scan was inspected across the introduction, Nueces geography, 1683–1716 records, Apache alliances, and the 1771 Taovayas discussion. Original manuscript sources and other works Bolton cites were not inspected.

Scholarly monographUniversity of Michigan Press / Museum of Anthropological Archaeology; digital edition at JSTORSource 6

Jumano and Patarabueye: Relations at La Junta de los Rios ↗

A specialist monograph compares Jumano and Patarabueye using documentary, linguistic, and archaeological evidence. Kelley’s distinctions and proposed correlations are scholarly interpretations, not settled ethnic identifications. Full institutional access is required; only the page metadata, chapter structure, and selected displayed excerpts were reviewed.

Inspection scope: Displayed excerpts from the introduction and selected chapters on historical data, Jumano identity, archaeology, and summary were read. JSTOR reported that the signed-in account lacked institutional access. The complete 201-page book was not inspected.

Historian discusses history of the Jumano nation ↗

A local report on a public talk by Jumano Nation of Texas members, including historian Felix Bonilla Salmeron. His statements about continuing Jumano identity and descendant-search efforts are attributed to him; the article is not an independent demographic or genealogical study.

Inspection scope: The full visible article body was read, including its direct quotations and image credit. A sign-in interface appeared below the story; the body was accessible without bypassing it. No underlying talk recording or independent genealogical evidence was inspected.

Preserving Our Ancestral Lands ↗

The organization describes its work and identifies Jumano among several descendant communities connected to La Junta. This is a first-party community self-description about its own broader community and stewardship; it does not establish that the organization is the Jumano Nation of Texas or speaks for all Jumano people.

Inspection scope: The visible homepage was read, including its self-description as Indigenous-led, named descendant communities, and discussion of current stewardship. The other named communities and individual family histories were not independently assessed.

Archaeology / educational synthesisTexas Beyond HistorySource 9

La Junta Reconsidered ↗

A separate educational synthesis about La Junta’s archaeology and changing interpretations. It explains why Jumano cannot simply stand for everyone who lived at or visited the confluence, and summarizes Kelley, Kenmotsu, and Morgenthaler models. Its statements about the disappearance of Native groups are attributed historical interpretations, not proof that descendant communities no longer exist.

Inspection scope: The full visible La Junta Reconsidered page was read, including its treatment of competing models and research limits. Cited books, archival material, and underlying archaeological data were not independently inspected.
